title: LlamaLab Pricing
summary: A clear look at LlamaLab pricing in 2026, including Basic plan request fees, setup costs, and Unlimited plan gaps, plus how Codes Health compares on completeness, verification, and flat fee pricing.
body_markdown:
If you are shopping for AI workflow automation software for medical record retrieval, the published price is only the starting point. LlamaLab markets itself as a flat fee alternative to traditional per page retrieval services, and that is a real advantage over per page billing. But price transparency on its own does not tell you whether the records will be complete, whether they will hold up in a courtroom, or whether the platform will actually fit the case management system your team already lives in. Before you commit to any retrieval partner, it is worth seeing how[Codes Health](https://www.getcodeshealth.com/) stacks up on the things that quietly decide case outcomes: record completeness, verification accuracy, and workflow integration that removes administrative overhead instead of adding to it.


## **Key Takeaways**


-


LlamaLab's Basic plan lists medical record requests at $50 each and billing record requests at $50 each, plus a $150 case setup fee per matter


-


LlamaLab's Core Unlimited plan includes unlimited medical and billing requests and waives the case setup fee, but the plan's total price is not published, so annual cost cannot be calculated without a quote


-


LlamaLab advertises a four day average retrieval time and roughly 30 to 40 percent same day returns, which are vendor reported figures rather than independently verified statistics


-


Codes Health works toward complete, litigation ready records in a couple of weeks, pairing AI validation with human review before records reach your desk


-


Incomplete authorizations are a leading cause of denied requests, and pre submission AI validation helps prevent the resubmissions that push timelines out


-


Codes Health's Filevine partnership lets teams submit requests, track status, and receive completed records without leaving the case file


## **Understanding LlamaLab's Transparent Pricing for Legal Workflow Automation**


LlamaLab positions itself as a transparently priced alternative to retrieval services that bill per page. Its published rates are set per request rather than per page, which contrasts against traditional services charging roughly $1 to $2 per page. For a 300 page record set, that difference can add up.


The per request rate does not tell the whole story, though. On the Basic plan, LlamaLab lists medical record requests at $50 each and billing record requests at $50 each, and adds a $150 case setup fee per matter. That distinction matters more than it might look. A case touching four facilities with one request each would run $350 including the setup fee. If your team requests both medical and billing records from all four of those facilities, the published request rates imply eight requests, or $400, plus the $150 setup fee, for a total of $550.


The Core Unlimited plan works differently. It lists unlimited per facility medical requests and unlimited per facility billing requests with a $0 case setup fee. LlamaLab does not publish the plan's total price, so firms cannot calculate an accurate annual cost without requesting a quote.


### **How LlamaLab Structures Retrieval Costs**


LlamaLab's model breaks into a few components:


-


**Medical record requests** : $50 each on the Basic plan, flat regardless of page count


-


**Billing record requests** : $50 each on the Basic plan, billed separately from medical requests


-


**Case setup fee** : $150 per case on Basic, waived on Core Unlimited


-


**Provider copy costs** : covered under LlamaLab's advertised flat per case option


-


**Rush fees** : not separately charged


-


**Platform or license fees** : none listed beyond retrieval costs


The retrieval only billing approach means the invoice can generally be recovered as a case expense at settlement rather than absorbed as firm overhead. That appeals to plaintiff firms that want operational costs tied to specific matters. One caveat worth raising during evaluation: LlamaLab's integration documentation refers to retrieval fees and provider charges being captured separately, so firms comparing Basic plan math should confirm exactly how third party provider charges are handled on their own account.


### **Speed Numbers and What They Actually Cover**


LlamaLab leans on speed in its marketing, advertising a four day average retrieval time and roughly 30 to 40 percent of records returned same day. Both are vendor reported. For firms used to waiting 30 to 90 days on traditional vendors, those numbers land.


Speed is genuinely useful, but it is worth asking what arrives in that window. Codes Health notes that services promising same day retrieval typically return only the records already available electronically, which leaves the rest of the treating history for the firm and the client to chase down. That added client involvement is the part that wears people out, and Codes Health says it is a meaningful driver of client churn. Records delivered fast but missing treatment dates, billing documentation, or an entire provider create gaps that defense counsel is happy to find for you.


[Codes Health](https://www.getcodeshealth.com/) takes the other side of that tradeoff. It works toward complete records in a couple of weeks and runs a Missing Record Review that compares returned materials against the original request and the available patient history. That check surfaces missing facilities, absent date ranges, and gaps in billing records before the set is treated as finished.


## **Evaluating Integration Depth for Healthcare Intake Workflows**


For personal injury firms, workflow automation software only pays off when it connects to the case management system your team already uses. Standalone platforms with separate logins, manual file transfers, and disconnected status tracking tend to move administrative work around rather than remove it.


### **LlamaLab's Integration Footprint**


LlamaLab documents native integrations with:


-


Litify, a deep integration with roughly a two week setup


-


Clio


-


Needles


-


SmartAdvocate, mentioned with limited public detail


LlamaLab also publicly documents an API architecture built to connect retrieval to case management systems, and a 2026 company article identifies Filevine as part of its integration roadmap. As of this writing, LlamaLab does not appear to publish a dedicated Filevine integration page comparable to its Litify documentation, so firms on Filevine should confirm the current state of that connection directly.


### **Why Filevine Integration Matters for Plaintiff Firms**


Filevine functions as a central operating environment where legal teams manage matters, documents, contracts, and workflows. When retrieval lives outside that environment, paralegals end up doing the following:


-


Logging into separate vendor portals to submit requests


-


Manually tracking status across disconnected systems


-


Downloading completed records and re uploading them to case files


-


Maintaining duplicate communication threads outside the case record


That fragmentation multiplies administrative time and creates compliance risk when the audit trail spans several systems.


Codes Health removes that friction through an[embedded Filevine workflow](https://www.getcodeshealth.com/) that lets legal teams:


-


Submit medical record requests directly from the relevant Filevine project


-


Track request status and provider outreach without leaving the case file


-


Communicate with the Codes Health team inside the Filevine workflow


-


Receive completed medical records, billing records, and associated materials back in the same project


Retrieval activity stays part of the case record from request through delivery, which supports both day to day efficiency and clean compliance documentation.


## **How AI Handles Medical Record Processing**


Both platforms use AI to speed up medical record processing. The implementation differences are what matter for litigation use.


### **AI Capabilities in Retrieval**


LlamaLab describes several AI powered features:


-


Reverse provider discovery using insurance claims data


-


OCR processing tuned for medical terminology


-


Clinical chronology generation


-


Portfolio intelligence for querying across case sets


-


Licensed clinical experts who validate AI output


LlamaLab also markets a completeness first approach, stating that it retrieves the complete treating history and uses provider discovery to identify providers a client left out at intake. Firms evaluating either platform should treat completeness as a process question rather than a marketing claim and ask exactly how each vendor confirms a record set is finished.


One thing worth separating out: general AI platforms like ChatGPT are not designed for litigation grade medical record review. They can summarize a document and pull basic information, but they lack the domain specific validation and verification a legal proceeding demands. Codes Health's platform is purpose built for this work and analyzes medical records with high precision, with AI output confirmed by specialists who understand both the medical terminology and the legal standard before anything reaches case strategy.


### **The Role of Human Verification**


Codes Health runs an AI and human hybrid workflow. Automated processing handles initial organization and extraction, then medical, legal, or operational specialists validate the findings.


That verification layer catches things pure automation misses:


-


Misidentified diagnoses or treatment codes


-


Incorrectly extracted dates or provider names


-


OCR errors in handwritten clinical notes


-


Missing pages or incomplete document sections


Codes Health differentiates further through Missing Record Review, which cross references returned materials against the request and the patient history to identify documentation gaps before retrieval is treated as complete.


Codes Health's MIT educated engineering team continuously builds out additional workflows and products, so the platform keeps evolving and getting more comprehensive as the demands of modern legal practices change.


### **Authorization Validation Prevents Costly Delays**


Incomplete authorizations are a leading cause of denied requests. Missing patient signatures, unclear expiration dates, or unchecked boxes for sensitive record categories send a request back and restart the provider response clock. Under the federal HIPAA right of access standard, a covered entity generally has 30 days to respond, with one possible 30 day extension, and shorter state level deadlines may apply. Attorney requests submitted under a signed authorization follow their own provider specific timelines, which is exactly why a rejected form is so expensive.


Codes Health's AI review catches these errors before submission. The system automatically flags:


-


Misspellings in patient or provider names


-


Missing dates of service


-


Signature issues that would cause a rejection


-


Provider specific requirements that vary by facility


Heading off the rejection and resubmission cycle is one of the least glamorous and most valuable things a retrieval partner can do.


## **Speed and Completeness Tradeoffs**


Understanding what drives LlamaLab's speed claims helps firms judge whether the approach fits their practice.


### **What Drives Fast Retrieval Times**


LlamaLab attributes its turnaround to several factors:


-


Direct connections to healthcare facilities


-


Healthcare entity status that bypasses standard queues


-


Automated follow up processes


-


Established provider relationships


These can meaningfully accelerate initial delivery compared with traditional fax and call retrieval.


### **When Speed Creates Risk**


Fast initial delivery becomes a problem when the record set is partial. A four day turnaround on an incomplete file creates false confidence, and the gaps often do not surface until deeper case review. By then, re requesting restarts the timeline and can collide with discovery deadlines. This is the same dynamic behind the churn issue with same day retrieval services: the client gets pulled back in to track down what did not arrive, and the firm absorbs the delay.


Codes Health verifies completeness before closing out a retrieval. When records look incomplete, the service works with the facility to resolve the gaps before returning the finished set. The goal is a package that is ready for litigation, not a starting point for more retrieval work.


### **Persistent Provider Follow Up**


Both platforms manage provider outreach. Codes Health's approach spans calls, faxes, emails, portals, and any other available channel until the requested materials arrive, with visibility into what outreach has already happened and what comes next rather than periodic vendor updates.


For facilities that routinely stall or need repeated contact, that persistence is what keeps a request from sitting in limbo while deadlines close in.


## **Evaluating Total Cost of Ownership**


Published request fees are one data point. Total cost also includes implementation effort, integration maintenance, and the downstream cost of incomplete or inaccurate records.


### **Comparing Retrieval Cost Structures**


Take a firm handling 100 cases a year with about four facilities per case.


**LlamaLab Basic plan:** With one request per facility, request fees come to $50 times four facilities times 100 cases, or $20,000, plus $150 in setup fees per case, or $15,000, for $35,000 annually. If the firm requests both medical and billing records at each facility, the published request rates would put request fees at $40,000, bringing the annual total to $55,000.


**LlamaLab Core Unlimited:** Unlimited medical and billing requests with the case setup fee waived. LlamaLab does not publish the plan price, so an annual figure cannot be calculated without a quote.


**Codes Health:** Flat fee per case, with no per page fees or provider pass through markups, and completeness verification included.


### **The Cost of Incomplete Records**


Cost math has to account for what happens when the first pass comes back short. Re requesting records, chasing additional provider outreach, and reconciling partial sets against case requirements all consume paralegal time that firms rarely track.


Gaps discovered during trial prep cost more still: rushed retrieval, possible continuance requests, and a weaker position when the missing documentation cannot be recovered in time. Codes Health's[Missing Record Review](https://www.getcodeshealth.com/) is designed to catch that during retrieval rather than during case preparation.


## **Usability Considerations for Integrated Retrieval**


LlamaLab positions its Litify and Clio integrations as enabling one click retrieval launch from the case management system. For firms on those platforms, that cuts manual data entry and keeps retrieval tied to the case file.


### **Integration Setup Requirements**


Implementing LlamaLab's Litify integration typically involves:


-


A working session with the firm's CMS admin and the LlamaLab team


-


Field mapping to align matter terminology


-


Document routing configuration


-


Roughly two weeks to go live


Firms running a document management layer such as Docrio on top of Litify need to coordinate additional routing so records land where the team expects them.


### **Where Codes Health Fits**


Codes Health's Filevine integration is available now, letting users validate authorizations, date ranges, and provider specific requirements before submission, then run the full retrieval lifecycle without leaving the Filevine project. For high volume customers that need deeper workflow customization, Codes Health also builds custom integrations with CRM platforms and other medical software beyond its standard platform partnerships.


## **Making an Informed Choice**


There is no single right answer here, but the decision usually comes down to a few honest questions about how your practice runs.


-


**How much of your caseload depends on complete treating history?** If damages, causation, or expert review hinge on catching every provider and date range, a systematic completeness process matters more than the fastest first delivery.


-


**What case management system do you actually use?** If your team runs on Litify or Clio, LlamaLab's documented integrations are a real fit. If Filevine is your system of record, Codes Health's embedded workflow keeps everything in the case file.


-


**Can you predict your annual spend?** Basic plan math changes substantially depending on whether you request billing records alongside medical records. Core Unlimited may be the better structure at volume, but you will need a quote to compare it against anything.


-


**Who absorbs the work when records come back incomplete?** If the answer is your paralegals or your clients, that cost belongs in the comparison even though it never shows up on an invoice.


Codes Health reports that firms using its platform see substantially less manual review time and greater case capacity. These are company reported customer outcomes, and individual results may vary.


## **The Bottom Line**


LlamaLab's published request pricing is a genuine improvement over per page billing, and its clinical validation and provider discovery features are more substantial than a speed first read of its marketing suggests. Where the comparison gets harder is cost predictability: the Basic plan's separate medical and billing request fees change the math considerably, and Core Unlimited's price is not public at all.


Codes Health competes on a different axis. Flat fee pricing, complete records in a couple of weeks, AI validation confirmed by human specialists, Missing Record Review before a retrieval is closed out, and an embedded Filevine workflow that keeps the whole process inside the case file. For firms whose cases live or die on complete treating history, that combination is where the value shows up.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **What does LlamaLab's Unlimited plan actually cost?**


LlamaLab's Core Unlimited plan lists unlimited per facility medical requests and unlimited per facility billing requests with a $0 case setup fee, but the plan's total price is not published. Firms need to contact LlamaLab for a quote before they can compare it against Basic plan pricing or any other vendor.


### **Can LlamaLab deliver certified records for trial admissibility?**


LlamaLab states that its retrieval process can include custodian certification, and its service materials indicate that chain of custody documentation accompanies record downloads. Attorneys should still confirm that the certification provided satisfies the evidentiary requirements of their specific jurisdiction and proceeding, particularly with a trial date approaching.


### **How does Codes Health handle facilities that routinely delay responses?**


Codes Health manages provider outreach across calls, faxes, emails, and portals until the requested materials arrive, with visibility into completed outreach attempts and the next required action. Firms can monitor progress without manually chasing updates, and persistent follow up keeps requests from stalling at unresponsive facilities while deadlines approach.


### **Does LlamaLab's pricing include provider copy costs?**


Provider copy costs are covered under LlamaLab's advertised flat per case option. Its integration documentation separately references retrieval fees and provider charges, so firms evaluating Basic plan pricing should confirm with LlamaLab how third party provider charges are handled for their specific account and record volumes.


### **What happens if Codes Health identifies missing records during completeness review?**


When completeness verification turns up gaps between returned materials and the original request, Codes Health works with the relevant facility to resolve them before closing the retrieval. The point is to hand the firm a finished record set rather than have missing documentation surface during case preparation or, worse, at trial.
